title: Tonkotsu Ramen
subtitle: Rich pork bone broth ramen with chashu pork and soft-boiled egg
excerpt: A home version of the Fukuoka classic: a thick, opaque pork bone broth built over several hours, poured over wavy ramen noodles and topped with rolled slices of slow-cooked pork belly, a soy-marinated soft egg, and a sheet of nori.

recipe.sourceNotes: Tonkotsu ramen originates from Fukuoka on the island of Kyushu, Japan, and is defined by its broth: a long-simmered pork bone stock cooked at a vigorous boil (unlike most stocks, which are simmered gently) until the collagen emulsifies and the liquid turns opaque, creamy, and intensely porky. The style spread nationally from the 1940s and is now one of the most internationally recognised ramen styles. Home versions of tonkotsu are time-consuming but achievable: the key is a rolling boil for the first several hours to drive the emulsification. The bowl is typically built with a seasoning base (tare) of soy sauce and mirin at the bottom, into which the hot broth is ladled; the ratio of tare to broth controls the final saltiness.

content.text: The broth must boil hard, not simmer: the vigorous boil emulsifies the pork fat into the water and is what makes tonkotsu white and creamy rather than clear. Blanch the bones before making the broth to remove blood and impurities. The chashu pork can be made in advance and refrigerated; sliced cold and then torched or griddled briefly before serving.

items.preparation: 600 g bones (pork trotters or neck bones if available) + 600 g rolled belly for chashu
for the tare and chashu marinade

content.text: Make the broth: blanch the pork belly and any bones in boiling water for 5 minutes. Drain and rinse. Return to the pot, cover with 3 litres of cold water, add the garlic, ginger, and spring onion. Bring to a vigorous boil and maintain a hard boil, partially covered, for 3 to 4 hours until the broth is opaque and creamy. Add water as needed to keep the bones submerged.

Remove the pork belly from the broth after 90 minutes (when cooked through but still holding shape). Roll tightly in cling film, refrigerate until cold. Mix the soy, mirin, and sake for the tare and marinating liquid. Soft-boil eggs for 6.5 minutes, cool in iced water, peel, and marinate in half the tare mixture for at least 2 hours.

Cook the noodles according to the packet. Strain the broth and season to taste. Place 1 tablespoon of tare in each bowl, ladle over 300 ml of hot broth, and add the noodles. Top with sliced chashu pork, halved marinated egg, bean sprouts, nori, and a drizzle of sesame oil. Scatter with sesame seeds.
